**Mode Collapse and Output Diversity in Language Models.** Neural language models are known to suffer from text degeneration, where maximization-based decoding produces repetitive, dull, and sometimes inconsistent outputs [1]. This problem, often termed mode collapse, has spurred a growing body of work on evaluating and improving output diversity. Holtzman et al. [1] identified the likelihood trap and proposed nucleus sampling (top-p) to mitigate degenerate repetition. Su et al. [2] attributed degeneration to the anisotropic token representation space and introduced contrastive training (SimCTG) paired with contrastive search decoding to jointly improve coherence and diversity. More recently, several benchmarks have been proposed to systematically evaluate LM diversity. Zhang et al. [3] introduced NoveltyBench, a benchmark curated to elicit diverse answers from both filtered real-world queries and synthetic prompts, finding that larger models within a family often exhibit less diversity. Le Bronnec et al. [4] adapted precision and recall metrics from image generation to text, revealing a quality-diversity trade-off that intensifies after instruction tuning and RLHF. Guo et al. [5] proposed a comprehensive framework for benchmarking linguistic diversity across lexical, syntactic, and semantic dimensions, showing that current alignment pipelines reduce output diversity. These works collectively establish that diversity is a fundamental shortcoming of modern LMs, yet most evaluations rely on narrow or synthetic tasks rather than capturing the full range of open-ended queries encountered in real-world usage.

**Open-Ended Generation Benchmarks and Datasets.** Several recent efforts have sought to build resources for evaluating LMs on creative and open-ended tasks using real-world interactions. Zhao et al. [6] released WildChat, a corpus of one million user-ChatGPT conversations spanning diverse languages and use cases, providing a valuable source of authentic user prompts. Wu et al. [7] introduced WritingBench, a benchmark covering six core writing domains with 100 subdomains, paired with a query-dependent evaluation framework for criteria-aware scoring. However, these resources are not specifically designed to systematically characterize the full spectrum of open-ended prompts that admit multiple valid responses, nor do they provide the dense, distributional human annotations needed to study pluralistic preference alignment.

**Decoding Strategies for Output Diversity.** Beyond benchmark-driven evaluation, substantial effort has focused on improving output diversity at the decoding stage. Zhang et al. [8] formalized decoding as a multi-objective quality-diversity optimization problem and conducted the first large-scale comparison of decoding algorithms, finding that all methods perform similarly when diversity is the priority. More recently, Minh et al. [9] proposed min-p sampling, a dynamic truncation method that scales the sampling threshold by the top token's probability, achieving improved diversity without sacrificing coherence at higher temperatures. Despite these advances, diversity-oriented decoding strategies place the burden on users to select appropriate configurations and are not broadly adopted, motivating solutions at the training level that robustly preserve output diversity by default.

**Cross-Model Homogenization and AI Safety Risks.** In parallel, a growing literature has examined how LM usage and synthetic data propagation can reduce content diversity at scale. Padmakumar and He [10] showed that collaborative writing with instruction-tuned LMs reduces both lexical and content diversity across different human authors. Briesch et al. [11] demonstrated that self-consuming training loops—where LMs are trained on their own outputs—lead to declining output diversity over successive generations. Guo et al. [12] corroborated this finding, showing that recursive fine-tuning on synthetic text causes consistent decreases in lexical, syntactic, and semantic diversity, especially on creative tasks. Rios-Sialer [13] framed homogenization as a primary AI safety concern and proposed structure-aware diversity pursuit as a mitigation strategy. While these studies highlight the risks of homogenization, they primarily focus on single-model settings or human-AI co-writing, leaving the systematic study of inter-model output convergence across diverse LMs relatively underexplored.

**Human Preference Alignment and Reward Modeling.** Aligning LMs with human preferences has become a central paradigm, driven by reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) [14] and direct preference optimization (DPO) [15]. These methods rely on reward models trained on human preference judgments, and their evaluation has been advanced by benchmarks such as RewardBench [16]. High-quality preference datasets such as HelpSteer2 [17] and HelpSteer3 [18] provide multi-attribute human annotations for training reward models, though they typically contain sparse annotations (e.g., 2–3 annotators per example). For scalable evaluation, LLM-based judges have emerged as a popular alternative: Prometheus [19] trains an open-source evaluator LM using fine-grained score rubrics, while Zheng et al. [20] introduced MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena to validate LLM-as-a-judge against human preferences. These pipelines, however, are predominantly designed and evaluated under the assumption that a single consensus notion of quality exists, potentially overlooking the diverse, idiosyncratic preferences that characterize open-ended user queries.

**Pluralistic Preferences and Annotator Disagreement.** Recognizing that human preferences are inherently heterogeneous, a nascent line of work has begun to move beyond consensus-based alignment. Bakker et al. [21] fine-tuned LMs to generate statements that maximize expected approval across groups with diverse opinions, demonstrating the feasibility of modeling population-level preference distributions. Padmakumar et al. [22] identified two key dimensions of subjectivity—plurality of valid responses and indistinguishability of paraphrases—and showed that standard reward models correlate weakly with aggregate user preferences in these cases. Zhang et al. [23] developed a taxonomy of disagreement sources in human preference annotations and found that standard reward models and LLM judges consistently produce decisive judgments even on examples with substantial annotator divergence. A recent survey by Xie et al. [24] provides a comprehensive overview of personalized and pluralistic preference alignment techniques. However, existing work in this direction is limited by the scarcity of datasets with dense, multi-annotator labels on open-ended queries, which are necessary to rigorously study the relationship between annotator disagreement, response diversity, and model calibration.

s2_metadata.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
s2_metadata.abstract:
Despite considerable advancements with deep neural language models, the enigma of neural text degeneration persists when these models are tested as text generators. The counter-intuitive empirical observation is that even though the use of likelihood as training objective leads to high quality models for a broad range of language understanding tasks, using likelihood as a decoding objective leads to text that is bland and strangely repetitive.\
  In this paper, we reveal surprising distributional differences between human text and machine text. In addition, we find that decoding strategies alone can dramatically effect the quality of machine text, even when generated from exactly the same neural language model. Our findings motivate Nucleus Sampling, a simple but effective method to draw the best out of neural generation. By sampling text from the dynamic nucleus of the probability distribution, which allows for diversity while effectively truncating the less reliable tail of the distribution, the resulting text better demonstrates the quality of human text, yielding enhanced diversity without sacrificing fluency and coherence.

tldr.text: [research paper] Neural text degeneration arises because language models' probability distributions have an unreliable tail of low-probability tokens that dominate under maximization-based decoding (e.g., beam search), leading to repetitive, incoherent outputs. Nucleus Sampling mitigates this by dynamically truncating the tail and sampling from the top-p probability mass, preserving both high-quality, diverse text and human-like variability—outperforming beam search, top-k sampling, and pure sampling in human and statistical evaluations.

s2_metadata.title: A Contrastive Framework for Neural Text Generation
s2_metadata.abstract: Text generation is of great importance to many natural language processing applications. However, maximization-based decoding methods (e.g. beam search) of neural language models often lead to degenerate solutions -- the generated text is unnatural and contains undesirable repetitions. Existing approaches introduce stochasticity via sampling or modify training objectives to decrease probabilities of certain tokens (e.g., unlikelihood training). However, they often lead to solutions that lack coherence. In this work, we show that an underlying reason for model degeneration is the anisotropic distribution of token representations. We present a contrastive solution: (i) SimCTG, a contrastive training objective to calibrate the model's representation space, and (ii) a decoding method -- contrastive search -- to encourage diversity while maintaining coherence in the generated text. Extensive experiments and analyses on three benchmarks from two languages demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art text generation methods as evaluated by both human and automatic metrics.

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper identifies that neural text generation degenerates due to anisotropic token representations—where tokens in a sentence have near-identical embeddings, leading to repetition. It proposes SimCTG, a contrastive training objective that enforces isotropic, discriminative token embeddings via contrastive learning, and contrastive search, a decoding method that selects high-probability tokens while preserving token sparsity to maintain coherence and diversity. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show superior performance over state-of-the-art methods in both automatic and human evaluations, with improved perplexity and reduced repetition.

s2_metadata.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
s2_metadata.abstract: Making language models bigger does not inherently make them better at following a user's intent. For example, large language models can generate outputs that are untruthful, toxic, or simply not helpful to the user. In other words, these models are not aligned with their users. In this paper, we show an avenue for aligning language models with user intent on a wide range of tasks by fine-tuning with human feedback. Starting with a set of labeler-written prompts and prompts submitted through the OpenAI API, we collect a dataset of labeler demonstrations of the desired model behavior, which we use to fine-tune GPT-3 using supervised learning. We then collect a dataset of rankings of model outputs, which we use to further fine-tune this supervised model using reinforcement learning from human feedback. We call the resulting models InstructGPT. In human evaluations on our prompt distribution, outputs from the 1.3B parameter InstructGPT model are preferred to outputs from the 175B GPT-3, despite having 100x fewer parameters. Moreover, InstructGPT models show improvements in truthfulness and reductions in toxic output generation while having minimal performance regressions on public NLP datasets. Even though InstructGPT still makes simple mistakes, our results show that fine-tuning with human feedback is a promising direction for aligning language models with human intent.

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper presents InstructGPT, a method for aligning large language models with human intent through reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). It combines supervised fine-tuning on human-written demonstrations with a reward model trained on human rankings of model outputs, then uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to refine the model. Results show that a 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT outperforms the 175B GPT-3 in human preference, truthfulness (halving hallucination rates), and toxicity (25% reduction), while maintaining minimal performance degradation on public NLP benchmarks—demonstrating that RLHF can effectively correct misalignment without significant task regressions.

references.raw_text: [15] R. Rafailov, A. Sharma, E. Mitchell, S. Ermon, C. D. Manning, and C. Finn. "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model." NeurIPS, 2023.
references.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model

s2_metadata.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
s2_metadata.abstract: While large-scale unsupervised language models (LMs) learn broad world knowledge and some reasoning skills, achieving precise control of their behavior is difficult due to the completely unsupervised nature of their training. Existing methods for gaining such steerability collect human labels of the relative quality of model generations and fine-tune the unsupervised LM to align with these preferences, often with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). However, RLHF is a complex and often unstable procedure, first fitting a reward model that reflects the human preferences, and then fine-tuning the large unsupervised LM using reinforcement learning to maximize this estimated reward without drifting too far from the original model. In this paper we introduce a new parameterization of the reward model in RLHF that enables extraction of the corresponding optimal policy in closed form, allowing us to solve the standard RLHF problem with only a simple classification loss. The resulting algorithm, which we call Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), is stable, performant, and computationally lightweight, eliminating the need for sampling from the LM during fine-tuning or performing significant hyperparameter tuning. Our experiments show that DPO can fine-tune LMs to align with human preferences as well as or better than existing methods. Notably, fine-tuning with DPO exceeds PPO-based RLHF in ability to control sentiment of generations, and matches or improves response quality in summarization and single-turn dialogue while being substantially simpler to implement and train.

tldr.text: [research paper] Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) replaces reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) with a closed-form, binary cross-entropy objective that directly optimizes language model policies to align with human preferences. By reparameterizing the RLHF objective using a change of variables, DPO eliminates the need for reward modeling, sampling, or complex policy updates—simplifying training while achieving performance comparable to or exceeding PPO-based RLHF in sentiment control, summarization, and dialogue tasks, with superior stability and computational efficiency.

s2_metadata.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
s2_metadata.abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) based chat assistants is challenging due to their broad capabilities and the inadequacy of existing benchmarks in measuring human preferences. To address this, we explore using strong LLMs as judges to evaluate these models on more open-ended questions. We examine the usage and limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, as well as limited reasoning ability, and propose solutions to mitigate some of them. We then verify the agreement between LLM judges and human preferences by introducing two benchmarks: MT-bench, a multi-turn question set; and Chatbot Arena, a crowdsourced battle platform. Our results reveal that strong LLM judges like GPT-4 can match both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences well, achieving over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans. Hence, LLM-as-a-judge is a scalable and explainable way to approximate human preferences, which are otherwise very expensive to obtain. Additionally, we show our benchmark and traditional benchmarks complement each other by evaluating several variants of LLaMA and Vicuna. The MT-bench questions, 3K expert votes, and 30K conversations with human preferences are publicly available at https://github.com/lm-sys/FastChat/tree/main/fastchat/llm_judge.

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper systematically evaluates LLM-as-a-judge using GPT-4 to approximate human preferences in open-ended, multi-turn dialogues, revealing over 80% agreement with human ratings across controlled expert and crowdsourced evaluations. It identifies and mitigates biases such as position, morbidity, and self-enhancement effects, demonstrating that LLM judges can reliably assess alignment with human preferences—enabling scalable, automated evaluation of conversational quality beyond traditional capability benchmarks.

references.title: Fine-tuning language models to find agreement among humans with diverse preferences

s2_metadata.title: Fine-tuning language models to find agreement among humans with diverse preferences
s2_metadata.abstract: Recent work in large language modeling (LLMs) has used fine-tuning to align outputs with the preferences of a prototypical user. This work assumes that human preferences are static and homogeneous across individuals, so that aligning to a a single "generic" user will confer more general alignment. Here, we embrace the heterogeneity of human preferences to consider a different challenge: how might a machine help people with diverse views find agreement? We fine-tune a 70 billion parameter LLM to generate statements that maximize the expected approval for a group of people with potentially diverse opinions. Human participants provide written opinions on thousands of questions touching on moral and political issues (e.g., "should we raise taxes on the rich?"), and rate the LLM's generated candidate consensus statements for agreement and quality. A reward model is then trained to predict individual preferences, enabling it to quantify and rank consensus statements in terms of their appeal to the overall group, defined according to different aggregation (social welfare) functions. The model produces consensus statements that are preferred by human users over those from prompted LLMs (>70%) and significantly outperforms a tight fine-tuned baseline that lacks the final ranking step. Further, our best model's consensus statements are preferred over the best human-generated opinions (>65%). We find that when we silently constructed consensus statements from only a subset of group members, those who were excluded were more likely to dissent, revealing the sensitivity of the consensus to individual contributions. These results highlight the potential to use LLMs to help groups of humans align their values with one another.

tldr.text: [research paper] This work fine-tunes a 70B-parameter LLM to generate consensus statements that maximize expected approval across a group of humans with diverse, potentially conflicting opinions—using a reward model trained on individual preference ratings and optimized via social welfare functions (e.g., utilitarian, egalitarian). Unlike prior alignment methods that assume homogeneous preferences, the model learns to synthesize group-level agreement by conditioning on collective input, producing statements preferred by humans over both prompted LLM outputs and top human-generated opinions (>65% preference), while revealing sensitivity to excluded individuals' views.

s2_metadata.title: A Survey on Personalized and Pluralistic Preference Alignment in Large Language Models

tldr.text: This survey introduces a taxonomy of personalized and pluralistic preference alignment in large language models (LLMs), distinguishing between training-time and inference-time methods that adapt LLM behavior to individual, contextual, and group-specific user preferences. It highlights that dynamic user preferences—such as tone, style, and response context—require methods like logit rectification, preference-based re-alignment, and user modeling, while emphasizing the lack of standardized benchmarks and open challenges in evaluating personalization effectiveness across diverse user scenarios.

\section{Related Work}
The diversity collapse problem of LMs. Diversity collapse, characterized by the inability of LMs to generate diverse outputs, presents a significant challenge to pluralistic alignment research [96, 78, 23, 93, 53, 91]. Prior studies identify some key factors contributing to diversity collapse, including training on synthetic data [33, 86, 93, 79], LM alignment [58, 41, 43], and insufficient diversity in training data [15]. Potential consequences of diversity collapse include reduced creativity, loss of minority perspectives, spread of bias, and overall decline in model utility and trustworthiness [5, 38, 21]. In response, a range of mitigation strategies are proposed, such as training corpora diversification [87, 68, 88, 34], training algorithm modifications [95, 54], alternative decoding [85, 62] and prompting [94, 11] strategies.

Measuring the creativity and divergent thinking of language models. Recent efforts to measure the creativity and divergent thinking of LMs often adapt established psychometric tests. For example, [16] utilizes a divergent association task (DAT) by asking models to generate semantically distant or unrelated words [63]. Similarly, tasks such as the Alternate Uses Test (AUT) [69], the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) [1, 13], Human Evaluation, and LLM-as-a-judge [46] are employed to assess dimensions like fluency, originality, complexity, and effective semantic diversity [80] of LM responses. Despite these demonstrated capabilities, LLM-generated creative content tends towards homogeneity, even when individual outputs achieve high creativity scores [90]. To address these evaluation complexities, some benchmarks, such as [72, 56, 66, 95], focus on specific creative abilities like scientific idea and code generation. Other works propose new metrics [61]. While LMs show promise in creative tasks, comprehensively evaluating their creativity remains an active and challenging research area [44]. We conduct a large-scale systematic study of real-world open-ended user queries and provide a comprehensive taxonomy, query dataset, and dense human annotations to improve evaluation and model training for reducing mode collapse in language models.

Disagreement and pluralistic alignment of language models. Advances in AI value alignment research have substantially improved LM utility and safety, through enhanced training processes [75, 64, 70], and the use of both synthetic data [30] and human datasets [8, 29]. Yet, a significant challenge remains: the potential for monolithic value representation [73, 74]. In contrast, the emerging focus on pluralistic alignment emphasizes the need for AI to serve the varied demands of a wide population [81, 2]. This shift is driving innovation in methods [19, 62, 49, 14, 26, 83], benchmarks [12], and data collection strategies [42, 76] to support this vision of diversity. Additionally, approaches leveraging multiple LMs interacting through system messages are also being explored to boost variety [84, 17, 59]. Parallel efforts are dedicated to quantifying and improving the cultural diversity exhibited by LLMs [71, 77, 18, 60, 52]. Yet, a common characteristic of many existing pluralistic alignment work is its reliance on predefined diversity dimensions, like demographics [48, 57], personality style [51, 35, 98, 65], and cultural background [92, 22, 4]. To enable models that genuinely cater to individuality without relying on stereotypes, individual-level alignment is needed [36, 98].

Potential consequences of diversity collapse include reduced creativity, loss of minority perspectives, spread of bias, and overall decline in model utility and trustworthiness [5, 38, 21]. In response, a range of mitigation strategies are proposed, such as training corpora diversification [87, 68, 88, 34], training algorithm modifications [95, 54], alternative decoding [85, 62] and prompting [94, 11] strategies.

Measuring the creativity and divergent thinking of language models. Recent efforts to measure the creativity and divergent thinking of LMs often adapt established psychometric tests. For example, [16] utilizes a divergent association task (DAT) by asking models to generate semantically distant or unrelated words [63]. Similarly, tasks such as the Alternate Uses Test (AUT) [69], the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) [1, 13], Human Evaluation, and LLM-as-a-judge [46] are employed to assess dimensions like fluency, originality, complexity, and effective semantic diversity [80] of LM responses. Despite these demonstrated capabilities, LLM-generated creative content tends towards homogeneity, even when individual outputs achieve high creativity scores [90]. To address these evaluation complexities, some benchmarks, such as [72, 56, 66, 95], focus on specific creative abilities like scientific idea and code generation. Other works propose new metrics [61]. While LMs show promise in creative tasks, comprehensively evaluating their creativity remains an active and challenging research area [44]. We conduct a large-scale systematic study of real-world open-ended user queries and provide a comprehensive taxonomy, query dataset, and dense human annotations to improve evaluation and model training for reducing mode collapse in language models.

Disagreement and pluralistic alignment of language models. Advances in AI value alignment research have substantially improved LM utility and safety, through enhanced training processes [75, 64, 70], and the use of both synthetic data [30] and human datasets [8, 29]. Yet, a significant challenge remains: the potential for monolithic value representation [73, 74]. In contrast, the emerging focus on pluralistic alignment emphasizes the need for AI to serve the varied demands of a wide population [81, 2]. This shift is driving innovation in methods [19, 62, 49, 14, 26, 83], benchmarks [12], and data collection strategies [42, 76] to support this vision of diversity. Additionally, approaches leveraging multiple LMs interacting through system messages are also being explored to boost variety [84, 17, 59]. Parallel efforts are dedicated to quantifying and improving the cultural diversity exhibited by LLMs [71, 77, 18, 60, 52]. Yet, a common characteristic of many existing pluralistic alignment work is its reliance on predefined diversity dimensions, like demographics [48, 57], personality style [51, 35, 98, 65], and cultural background [92, 22, 4]. To enable models that genuinely cater to individuality without relying on stereotypes, individual-level alignment is needed [36, 98].

s2_metadata.title: Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper presents a comprehensive study of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for training language models to be helpful and harmless. It introduces an iterated online RLHF training process where preference models and policies are updated weekly with fresh human feedback, leading to sustained improvements in both helpfulness and harmlessness. A key finding is a roughly linear relationship between the RL reward and the square root of the KL divergence between policy and initialization, indicating a predictable trade-off in policy divergence. The results show that RLHF does not degrade performance on most NLP tasks—especially for larger models—and can be effectively combined with specialized skill training (e.g., code generation) without compromising alignment or capability.

claims.text: Neural language models suffer from text degeneration due to maximization-based decoding, producing repetitive and dull outputs.
Holtzman et al. identified the likelihood trap and proposed nucleus sampling (top-p) to mitigate degenerate repetition.
Su et al. attributed degeneration to anisotropic token representations and introduced SimCTG with contrastive search decoding.
Zhang et al. introduced NoveltyBench for eliciting diverse answers, finding larger models exhibit less diversity.
Le Bronnec et al. adapted precision and recall metrics to text, revealing a quality-diversity trade-off that intensifies after instruction tuning and RLHF.
Guo et al. proposed a framework for benchmarking linguistic diversity across lexical, syntactic, and semantic dimensions.
Zhao et al. released WildChat, a corpus of one million user-ChatGPT conversations.
Wu et al. introduced WritingBench covering six writing domains with 100 subdomains and a query-dependent evaluation framework.
Existing open-ended generation benchmarks do not characterize the full spectrum of prompts nor provide dense annotations for pluralistic alignment.
Zhang et al. formalized decoding as a multi-objective quality-diversity optimization, finding all algorithms perform similarly when diversity is prioritized.

retrieved_evidence.text: [research paper] HelpSteer2 introduces a compact, permissively licensed preference dataset (10k response pairs) trained on diverse real-world prompts from ShareGPT, augmented with enterprise-relevant use cases and generated via multiple internal LLMs (Nemotron-2/3/4, Mixtral) and human annotators. The dataset enables state-of-the-art reward modeling (92.0% on Reward-Bench), outperforming existing open and proprietary models, and supports SteerLM 2.0—an alignment method that leverages multi-attribute rewards to train LLMs on complex, multi-requirement instructions, improving alignment fidelity in real-world scenarios.

High-quality preference datasets are essential for training reward models that can effectively guide large language models (LLMs) in generating high-quality responses aligned with human preferences. As LLMs become stronger and better aligned, permissively licensed preference datasets, such as Open Assistant, HH-RLHF, and HelpSteer need to be updated to remain effective for reward modeling. Methods that distil preference data from proprietary LLMs such as GPT-4 have restrictions on commercial usage imposed by model providers. To improve upon both generated responses and attribute labeling quality, we release HelpSteer2, a permissively licensed preference dataset (CC-BY-4.0). Using a powerful internal base model trained on HelpSteer2, we are able to achieve the SOTA score (92.0%) on Reward-Bench's primary dataset, outperforming currently listed open and proprietary models, as of June 12th, 2024. Notably, HelpSteer2 consists of only ten thousand response pairs, an order of magnitude fewer than existing preference datasets (e.g., HH-RLHF), which makes it highly efficient for training reward models. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that reward models trained with HelpSteer2 are effective in aligning LLMs. In particular, we propose SteerLM 2.0, a model alignment approach that can effectively make use of the rich multi-attribute score predicted by our reward models. HelpSteer2 is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/HelpSteer2 and code is available at https://github.com/NVIDIA/NeMo-Aligner

It achieves state-of-the-art performance on RM-Bench (82.4%) and JudgeBench (73.7%) by training Reward Models on human-annotated data, outperforming prior datasets by ~10% absolute, and enables effective alignment of policy models via RLHF without relying on GPT-4 or restricted licensing.

Preference datasets are essential for training general-domain, instruction-following language models with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Each subsequent data release raises expectations for future data collection, meaning there is a constant need to advance the quality and diversity of openly available preference data. To address this need, we introduce HelpSteer3-Preference, a permissively licensed (CC-BY-4.0), high-quality, human-annotated preference dataset comprising of over 40,000 samples. These samples span diverse real-world applications of large language models (LLMs), including tasks relating to STEM, coding and multilingual scenarios. Using HelpSteer3-Preference, we train Reward Models (RMs) that achieve top performance on RM-Bench (82.4%) and JudgeBench (73.7%). This represents a substantial improvement (~10% absolute) over the previously best-reported results from existing RMs. We demonstrate HelpSteer3-Preference can also be applied to train Generative RMs and how policy models can be aligned with RLHF using our RMs. Dataset (CC-BY-4.0): https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/HelpSteer3#preference Models (NVIDIA Open Model): https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/reward-models-68377c5955575f71fcc7a2a3
